title: Score blind first, then reveal
body: Collect every judge's scores before anything is shared, then show only the aggregates. Keep both scores so herding can be measured directly: a judge moving towards the consensus with no new evidence is conforming, not updating. Herding is strongest when peers' reasons are shown and a judge is unsure.

title: Ground every candidate in the same evidence dossier
body: Research each hypothesis or name the same way (literature search, database checks, prior art) before judging, and tell the judges to rely on it. This league did that. It counters the 'novelty mirage', where LLM judges rate machine ideas as more novel than experts do. It is how AI co-scientist's reflection agent works.

title: Hide authorship and normalise style
body: Judges prefer their own output and are swayed by length and polish. Anonymise entries, cap pitches, and optionally have one cheap model rewrite every entry into a fixed template before judging. In one study, style normalisation raised substance recognition from 0.50 to 0.76.

title: Use an anchored multi-criterion rubric
body: Score novelty, feasibility, significance and testability separately, each with anchored level descriptions, and combine them with stated weights. Absolute rubric scores resist assertive wording better than pairwise preferences: 9% of verdicts flipped rather than 35%.

title: Rank the finalists pairwise, with Bradley-Terry and Swiss pairing
body: Filter a large field with absolute scores, then rank the top with pairwise comparisons fitted by Bradley-Terry. Swiss pairing recovers the true order better than knockout halving for the same number of comparisons. Show both orders to cancel position bias.

title: Buy independence, not headcount
body: Judges trained on similar data make correlated errors: in one study nine frontier judges were worth about two independent votes. Measure the effective number of judges, as this report does, and prefer diverse model families over more copies of similar ones. A small diverse panel beat a single large judge at a seventh of the cost.

title: Pay predictions with a proper scoring rule
body: A flat reward for picking the eventual winner rewards bandwagoning, because the leader is the safest pick. Ask for a probability over the field each round and score it with a log or Brier rule. Without ground truth, 'surprisingly popular' or peer-prediction scoring still rewards honest reports.

title: Add a calibrated, non-verbal judge
body: A decision model that returns probabilities, like Jev, is cheap, cannot be talked round by rhetoric, and its errors are less correlated with chat models'. Use it on narrow, well-anchored questions and as a tiebreaker, and weigh it by its measured agreement with experts.

title: Keep debate short
body: Majority voting explains most of multi-agent debate's gains, and long debates lock agents into their first positions. One advocacy round for the survivors, as in this league, gets most of the benefit for the fewest tokens.

title: Plant controls and repeat runs
body: Seed a known-weak candidate (and, where possible, a known-strong one) to check the panel is discriminating and not colluding. Repeat with different seeds and orders, and report how often each candidate wins instead of a single winner.

title: Close the loop with execution and experts
body: Judged quality is not realised quality. Once LLM research ideas were executed, their scores fell further than human ideas' and the ranking often reversed. Treat the league as a triage filter and send the top few to an experiment, a simulation or an expert review. For names, that means a trade-mark search and a customer test.
